cards.title: Choose headline and body type size for on-screen readability
cards.summary: Pick initial-cap headlines, Arial/Verdana sizing, and dark-on-light color to maximize online reading speed for ads and landing pages.
cards.use_when: Formatting headlines, body copy or a landing-page hero for on-screen reading (PDP, ad, email) where legibility affects completion.
steps: Set headlines in initial caps, not all caps. All-caps words form uniform rectangular outlines so the eye has fewer distinctive shapes to recognize, slowing reading; source cites an 18.9% gap favoring initial caps and Tinker's finding that all caps slowed reading.

For body text 12pt and larger, use Arial; below 12pt prefer Verdana but rarely go below 10pt. For a formal look use Georgia; for older audiences use 14pt. These come from multiple online legibility studies (Tullis/Boynton/Hersh; Bernard/Mills; Bernard et al.; Software Usability Research Laboratory), which the author synthesizes into one recommendation.
Set long headlines in black on white; white backgrounds read best, then yellow. Avoid reversing text out of dark backgrounds for long passages.
Remember paper and screen differ: print is ~300 dpi while Mac screens are ~72 dpi and Windows ~96 dpi, so a font that reads well in print may not read well online.
Verify current font availability and rendering on your actual storefront templates before standardizing, since interfaces change.
caveats: Recommendations are the author's synthesis of older readability studies, not a current controlled test of your audience or device mix.
Preference and speed results from these studies were sometimes mixed, so treat point sizes as heuristics, not hard rules.

cards.title: Hire a real designer instead of self-designing sales materials
cards.summary: Use a vetted freelance designer or art-school student and always review samples before paying, because graphic software skills are not design skill.
cards.use_when: Producing product images, ad creative, packaging or sales collateral where amateur design risks a low-quality brand impression.
steps: Recognize the source's claim: owning design software does not make you a designer, and amateurish materials damage your image especially with prospects who don't know you.

To find a designer, call local ad agencies and ask to speak with the art or creative director, explaining you run a small business putting together an ad/brochure/flyer and asking for freelance recommendations; agencies usually work with several.

If hiring online, review the portfolio, ask the rate, and confirm whether billing is hourly or per project. Rates vary and some designers price by how large they think your company is, so the source advises not sounding big.
If budget is tight, call local graphic-arts schools for students who will work cheaply.
Before paying anyone, request samples; some will be excellent, others poor.
Note this card concerns creative production quality, not ad-media buying.
caveats: The source's remark that designers may charge based on perceived company size is an anecdotal opinion, not a pricing rule.
There is no implied benchmark for what a good designer costs.

cards.title: Use questions to pull readers through copy
cards.summary: Open headlines, subheads and body copy with questions, especially 'Do you want...?' followed by a benefit, to keep prospects reading.
cards.use_when: Writing a product page, ad, email or sales letter where you need to hold attention from the headline into the body.
steps: Place questions in headlines, subheads and body copy. The source's stated mechanism is that a question creates an 'open loop' the reader wants to close, so they keep reading for the answer.
Use 'Do you want...?' openers followed immediately by a strong benefit, e.g., 'Do you want to DOUBLE, TRIPLE, even QUADRUPLE your self-confidence?'
Treat each sentence's job as earning the next: the purpose of the first sentence and paragraph is to get people to read the second.
Use questions as mini pop-quizzes in long-form content to keep readers alert and to make monologue feel like two-way conversation.
Note the source admits there is no scientific research supporting the NLP open-loop claim; the technique's justification is his observed readership effect.
caveats: Open-loop/NLP framing is attributed to NLP proponents only, without scientific support per the source itself.
Overusing questions can feel gimmicky; the source does not set a maximum.

cards.title: Make sales letters personal, brochures detailed
cards.summary: Treat the sales letter as a one-on-one salesperson that meets prospects in their world, and the brochure as the sample-filled briefcase of complete details.
cards.use_when: Planning an email or sales letter versus a catalog/brochure, or deciding how personal versus detailed each piece of a campaign should be.
steps: Divide roles: the letter is the personal salesperson establishing rapport; the brochure is the impersonal briefcase of photos, samples and complete detail. Both work toward the same sale.

Write to 'meet the prospect in their world' by reflecting their language, age and situation. The source contrasts a stiff 'Dear Justin: The weekend is young...' opening against a casual 'Hey Justin... if you're sick and tired of staying home...' opening.
List every benefit first (not features), then rank them by importance to the customer, not to you. Put the #1 benefit in the opening of the letter.

Personalize salutations. 'Dear Bob' beats 'Dear Friend'; when you cannot personalize, use a transformation salutation like 'Dear Weekend Warrior' or 'Dear Soon-to-Be-Millionaire.' Never use 'Dear Occupant.'
Work the ideas of ease and quickness into the first sentence where relevant, since the source argues buyers respond to speed and ease.
caveats: These formatting prescriptions are the author's direct-marketing conventions; email and privacy norms may restrict personalization data today.
The source's example testimonial copy is illustrative, not a tested result.

cards.title: Write teasers that survive the trash can
cards.summary: Design outer envelopes/carrier copy to look personal, not informational, so prospects open before trashing.
cards.use_when: Designing the subject line and sender presentation for a direct-mail or email campaign to a cold or loosely targeted list.
steps: Assume most mail is trashed within seconds and that many people open mail over a trash can, so you have only moments to grab attention.

Prefer nonspecific teasers such as 'PERSONAL ATTENTION OF:', 'PERSONAL LETTER FOR:' or 'IMPORTANT LETTER FOR:' over informational teasers. Informational teasers announce 'this is a sales pitch,' so the source advises using them only when the list is pin-point targeted to the offer.
Use physical cues that signal personal mail: brightly colored envelopes, a bloodred 'URGENT' stamp, and multiple small-denomination stamps instead of one stamp.

Write a personalized note next to the typed name, e.g., 'Eileen: Here's the Information We Talked About! —Drew,' or with an implied deadline such as 'Please Read This Letter Before 9:30 Tonight,' justifying the deadline in the letter.
Do not use mailing labels; they signal mass mailing. Feed envelopes through a printer, use a realistic handwriting font, or have a seniors group hand-address them.
caveats: Personal-looking tactics may conflict with spam regulations or brand standards in email; adapt carefully.
The source's preference for nonspecific teasers assumes the mailing list is not precisely targeted.

cards.title: Build a Granny-style response device
cards.summary: Convert order forms into warm, easy-to-complete 'Personal Trial Certificates' with guarantee, scarcity and a business reply envelope.
cards.use_when: Designing a cart, order form or checkout page to reduce friction and lift completion rate.
steps: Rename the response device: instead of 'Order Form,' call it a 'Personal Trial Certificate' or 'Personal, No-Obligation Trial Certificate.'
Pre-fill the recipient's name and address. Print it on canary (yellow) paper so it stands out from other pieces.
Restate the offer on the form and place a bold 'YES!' check next to a box. The source cites John Caples' advice to show a small picture of what the buyer receives.
Play up the guarantee prominently, and put your mailing address, phone and web/email on the bottom in case the reader loses the rest. Put your name and address on all components.
Add scarcity and a deadline on the form itself, plus everywhere else in the mailing; without a deadline people tend to 'think about it.'
Include a business reply envelope (or a live stamp if you lack a reply permit), rubber-stamping 'RUSH! ORDER ENCLOSED!' or '24-HOUR PROCESSING' in red.
caveats: This is designed for direct mail; adapt the equivalent cart elements rather than literally mailing reply envelopes.
The source's claims about pre-filled forms and deadlines are his conventions, not measured benchmarks.

cards.title: Collect testimonials systematically with permission
cards.summary: Request testimonials with a specific questionnaire and a signed usage release, compensating with copies of the finished piece or a small payment.
cards.use_when: Sourcing social proof for a product page, ad or brochure and needing documented permission to use customer quotes.
steps: Email or write customers: 'We want to make you famous!' and ask for their honest opinions for a new ad, brochure or website, offering, if they like, their photo.

Ask questions that produce quotable specifics, e.g., what they think of the service, what kind of response they get, how you compare to other providers, what they like best, whether prices are reasonable, and whether they'd recommend or hire you again.
Include a permission line granting you rights to use the quotes in complete or edited form, with checkboxes for with/without name and city/state, plus a signature and date line.

Provide consideration: the source says sending copies of the first printed piece in which the testimonial appears legally binds the agreement, or alternatively enclose $1.00 to cover their return expenses.
Pay the return postage with a self-addressed stamped envelope so the customer incurs no expense.
Always send the promised copies of the finished piece.
caveats: The source's description of 'consideration' is a lay legal explanation, not legal advice; confirm testimonial consent and compensation rules for your jurisdiction and platform.

cards.title: Use the Guillotine Principle to grab attention with a face
cards.summary: Place a close-up human face looking directly at the reader in ads and pages to gain attention, warmth and trust.
cards.use_when: Choosing the main image for an ad, PDP, packaging or landing-page hero where stopping power and warmth matter.
steps: Add a photo of a person's head or face, looking directly at the reader. Faces are described as the best attention-getters.
Choose expression based on context: smiling is generally preferable, but a screaming, distorted face would be a shocker appropriate to a product like tear gas.
Show the founder's face for service and craft businesses (carpenter, dentist) to add warmth and convert a faceless business into a real person.
Even a tiny black-and-white photo will do; keep it simple.
Put the photo at the top of the ad and make the headline a quote from you, e.g., a headline reading 'Give Me 90 Minutes & I'll Show You How to Double...Triple...Quadruple Your Ad Response!'
Repeat your photo and name across ads; the source claims repeated exposure can build recognition over time.
caveats: Faces draw attention but the source gives no measured conversion lift; test against your audience and product.
A face that mismatches the offer's emotional tone can undercut the ad.

cards.title: Sharpen copy with powerful visual adjectives (PVAs)
cards.summary: Replace generic product descriptions with concrete, sensory adjectives that let prospects picture and mentally demo the product.
cards.use_when: Rewriting commodity product or service descriptions where your offer looks like competitors' and needs to stand out.
steps: Swap bland descriptions for concrete imagery. The source's examples: 'Make lots of money' becomes 'Rake in $2,750 cash weekly'; 'Juicy red apples' becomes 'Mouth-watering, sugar-sweet, hand-picked apples'; 'Drink cleaner water' becomes 'Enjoy pure, crystal-clear, glacier-fresh water.'
For a specialty soap, describe the experience as splashing skin with 'liquid sunshine' or sliced Florida oranges, and rename a 'lather' as 'Sweet Orange-Cream Bubbles.'

Use the same technique for services: instead of 'Our expert cleaners will make your office sparkle like new,' specify walls and floors 'hospital-bright,' restrooms 'sparkling and sanitized,' carpets 'fluffy, fresh, and deodorized.'

The source's stated rationale: specific sensory words create clearer mental pictures and make you look more qualified and conscientious than competitors who tell only part of the story, so competitors appear to do less.
Apply to your weakest, most generic product copy first and compare response.
caveats: Source's claims of competitive advantage are persuasive argument, not tested data, and his own soap colleague pushed back that it was over the top.
Do not let PVAs override truth or compliance on claims like income or health.

cards.title: Direct mental movies through the five senses (VAKOG)
cards.summary: Ramp up sensory detail across visual, auditory, kinesthetic, olfactory and gustatory channels so prospects mentally rehearse using the product before buying.
cards.use_when: Writing long-form sales copy, product pages or emails that must move a prospect from facts to purchase.
steps: Recognize that all experience blends five elements: Visual (sight), Auditory (sound), Kinesthetic (feeling/emotion), Olfactory (smell), Gustatory (taste). The source calls them internal representations (IRs).
Write to intensify these IRs so the reader experiences your product internally. Facts alone create few IRs and won't prime buying, per the source's pool-cleaner example.

Tour prospects through the product: name it, describe how it looks, sounds, feels and how using it changes their day. The source's pool-cleaner letter describes a hose like a 'blue manta ray,' a 'chuga-chuga-chuga' sound, sparkling water that 'smells better,' and piped-in 'piña coladas.'
Not every sense applies to every product; a printer won't sell taste, but can describe paper's smooth or cottony texture and how it feels to hold the stationery, creating quality associations.
Consider a 'step-out' authenticity move: a line that momentarily steps outside the ad to convey real-time, here-and-now genuineness.
Use this to justify longer copy; the source claims longer copy outsells short because it accumulates more IRs.
caveats: VAKOG and the long-copy claim are stated as the author's experience, not measured universal benchmarks; test against your audience.
Ethical and regulatory limits apply to exaggerated sensory promises and guarantees.

cards.title: Battle inertia by making buying easy and asking for action
cards.summary: Lower effort on every step and make an explicit call to action, since people are lazy and avoid involvement.
cards.use_when: Optimizing checkout, signup, quote request or any conversion flow where prospects stall or abandon.
steps: Follow the source's two-step formula: make it easy to act, then ask for action. He warns these do not guarantee action but raise the odds.
Offer pre-filled forms where practical (name, address, credit card slot) and a postage-paid reply; remove roadblocks so the prospect says 'Gee, look how easy!'
Accept as many alternate payment forms as possible (major credit cards, checks, money orders, PayPal) and offer several shipping speeds, from ground to overnight.
Offer gift-wrapping, a strong guarantee to quell fear of loss, and payment plans like 'Just $14.99 a month for three months' to reduce the pain of spending.
Tell prospects exactly how to order, step by step; for retailers give address, phone, driving directions and hours.
Use phrase variants like 'It's Easy To Order!' or 'It's Easy to Get a FREE Estimate!' for your context.
caveats: This is the source's sales principle, not a guarantee; he explicitly disclaims that following these steps produces universal success.
Pre-filled and stored payment details carry privacy/security obligations today, unlike direct mail.

cards.title: Differentiate with a unique selling proposition (USP)
cards.summary: Craft a real, truth-based gimmick or system that distinguishes your offer, since indistinguishable products give buyers no reason to prefer you.
cards.use_when: Positioning a product or store in a crowded category where your offer reads like generic sugar or salt.
steps: Accept the source's premise: when people can't distinguish you from competitors, they have no reason to prefer you. Commodity products get no preference.

Find or build a genuine differentiator and name it. Examples: not a hardware store but 'The Hardware Superstore!'; not an office cleaner but 'The Office Cleaning Technicians!'; not a real estate office but the 'Experts of the RapidSell System!'
If you don't have a named system, the source says create a real program you can name, so the USP reflects what's true.

Study his Nifty Fifty's diner example: they announce never using frozen beef, grinding burgers fresh daily, fresh-cut fries, no frozen onion rings, visible kitchen prep and the frying oil used. They are proactive about telling customers why they are great instead of hoping customers discover it.
Make sure the product or service is genuinely excellent, or you may educate buyers away from you.
caveats: The source stresses positioning should reflect what's true; an invented claim you can't back will backfire.
This is the author's opinion-driven framework; no conversion benchmarks are offered.
